items.readable_text:
Content:
A piecewise function is a function that is defined differently in different parts of the function's domain.

Content:
For example, consider the piecewise function [MATH: f(x),] defined as follows:
[MATH: {− 2x,|x ≤ 0; (1)/(2)x,|x > 0]
A plot of the function is given below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ec3909ca0441a873e1289e20fc7d3ea]

Content:
The function has two distinct branches, one for [MATH: \color{red}{x\leq 0}] and one for [MATH: \color{blue}{x>0}.] The function is a piecewise function because it has different definitions depending on where we are in the domain.

Content:
Suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: f(-1).] For this, we'd use the left branch [MATH: x \leq 0] because [MATH: -1 \leq 0.] On this branch, the function definition is [MATH: f(x) = -2x,] so we have

Content:
[MATH: f(-1) = -2(-1) = 2.]

Content:
Similarly, if we want to calculate [MATH: f(1)], we'd use the right branch [MATH: x > 0] because [MATH: 1 > 0.] On this branch, the function definition is [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x,] so we have

Content:
[MATH: f(1) = \dfrac 1 2 \cdot 1 = \dfrac 1 2.]

The function is defined for values between [MATH: -4] and [MATH: 1.]

  • Since there is an open circle at [MATH: x=-4,] this point is not included in the domain.

  • Since there is a closed circle at [MATH: x=-1,] this point is included in the domain.

  • Since there is an open circle at [MATH: x=1,] this point is not included in the domain.

So, the function [MATH: f(x)] above is defined for values between [MATH: x=-4] and [MATH: x=1,] not including [MATH: x=-4] and [MATH: x=1] but including [MATH: x=-1.]

Therefore, the domain is [MATH: x\in (-4,1)]

Note that the function is defined at the point [MATH: x=-1,] even though the function jumps at that point. The function value at [MATH: x=-1] is [MATH: 2.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
A piecewise function is a function that is defined differently in different parts of the function's domain.

Content:
For example, consider the piecewise function [MATH: f(x),] defined as follows:
[MATH: {− 2x,|x ≤ 0; (1)/(2)x,|x > 0]
A plot of the function is given below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3ec3909ca0441a873e1289e20fc7d3ea]

Content:
The function has two distinct branches, one for [MATH: \color{red}{x\leq 0}] and one for [MATH: \color{blue}{x>0}.] The function is a piecewise function because it has different definitions depending on where we are in the domain.

Content:
Suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: f(-1).] For this, we'd use the left branch [MATH: x \leq 0] because [MATH: -1 \leq 0.] On this branch, the function definition is [MATH: f(x) = -2x,] so we have

Content:
[MATH: f(-1) = -2(-1) = 2.]

Content:
Similarly, if we want to calculate [MATH: f(1)], we'd use the right branch [MATH: x > 0] because [MATH: 1 > 0.] On this branch, the function definition is [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x,] so we have

Content:
[MATH: f(1) = \dfrac 1 2 \cdot 1 = \dfrac 1 2.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating Piecewise Functions

Example Prompt:
For the function [MATH: g(x)] defined on the set of integers, find [MATH: g(-12)] and [MATH: g(3),] where [MATH: g(x)] is the following piecewise function:
[MATH: {2x,|x < 1; 3x,|x ≥ 1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
- First, we compute [MATH: g(-12).] Since [MATH: -12 < 1,] we use the first branch:
[MATH: g(x)|= 2x; g(− 12)|= 2(− 12); = − 24]
- Next, we compute [MATH: g(3).] Since [MATH: 3 \geq 1,] we use the second branch:
[MATH: g(x)|= 3x; g(3)|= 3(3); = 9]

- Since there is an open circle at [MATH: x=1,] this point is not included in the domain.

[MATH: x\in (-4,1)]
